newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo sides accuse each other of war of nerves.
newsitem.headline: Congo sides accuse each other of war of nerves.

text.p: Congo's warring parties accused each other of a shooting war of nerves on Tuesday after fresh shelling rocked the capital Brazzaville.
Artillery fire boomed in the afternoon across the city where a ceasefire since Saturday has merely lessened the intensity of combat.

A month-long civil war, which has killed hundreds in the capital, began when President Pascal Lissouba tried to arrest his rival and immediate predecessor in office, Denis Sassou Nguesso, and disarm his private army.
"The others are firing a bit all over the place. They are trying to grind people down. They are not actually targetting anything," a spokesman for Lissouba told Reuters by telephone.
Sassou's aides made a similar claim about their foes who they also accused of ferrying in Serb, Liberian and Angolan UNITA mercenaries to shore up their power.

France's Raymond Cesaire, the only ambassador left, said on Monday fighting near his embassy, in the deserted city centre still strewn with weeks-old corpses, did not involve the two sides in a direct battle to make gains.
"It seems to involve battles between bands of looters or soldiers letting off steam, rather than a threat or a deliberate break of the ceasefire by one side or the other," he said.
Bernard Kolelas, the city mayor who is trying to mediate, met Lissouba, the presidency said, but the armed camps seemed as far apart as ever.

Lissouba wants a constitutional commission to extend for three months his term in office which began in 1992 when he defeated Sassou in free elections and was due to end with a now postponed poll on July 27.
Sassou, who was to have stood against him in the election, says this is impossible. He says the state and army have crumbled away and demands power-sharing for an interim period.

"There is no provision in the constitution to extend Lissouba's mandate. It would solve nothing. In three months it would be impossible to repair what has been destroyed," his spokesman Francois Ibovi told Reuters.
"In three months it would be impossible to recreate conditions conducive to free and fair elections."
Lissouba, in a show of confidence, briefly left his warring Congo for the first time on Monday for a visit over the Congo river to Laurent Kabila's Kinshasa.
The former colonial Brazzaville, wartime capital for "Free French" leader General Charles de Gaulle, has been devastated by shelling, street battles and looting since June 5.
Aid workers, who have now left, estimate some 1,000 to 3,000 people, mostly civilians, have died. Some of the heaviest fighting has been for the city airport.

International mediation efforts led by Omar Bongo, president of neighbouring Gabon, have centred on the dispatch of an African intervention force but the United Nations says there must be a lasting peace first in oil-rich Congo.
